newsitem.title: TAIWAN: FORECAST-Taiwan May jobless rate seen at 2.65 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Taiwan May jobless rate seen at 2.65 pct.

text.p: A Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists on Friday projected Taiwan's May joblessness would come in at 2.65 percent, a slight rise from April due chiefly to job losses from a hog farm epidemic.
The figures were due to be released at 0300 GMT on June 23 by the Directrate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics.
April's jobless rate was 2.59 percent.
The following table lists institutions' forecasts for May unemployment in percent:
Institution forecast
Core Pacific Securities 2.73
Grand Cathay Securities 2.57
HSBC James Capel Taiwan 2.65
National Securities 2.7
Nomura Securities 2.6
Average 2.65

Economists said they expected May joblessness to rise slightly from April due to job losses on Taiwan's feedlots, where a late March outbreak of hog foot-and-mouth disease forced a ban on pork exports -- a US$1.5 billion a year business before the blight -- and the slaughter of four million pigs.
"The impact of the hog epidemic should be clear in May's jobless rate, likely pushing up the rate slightly," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
Directorate officials in May sought to ease early concerns that the epidemic could cause huge job losses, saying more recent signs pointed to far less impact.
"The unemployed population will not increase sharply (due to the hog crisis)," statistics agency director Chen Chang-hsiung said at the time.
Economists initially reckoned that the pork export ban could throw 50,000 or even 100,000 workers out of jobs, adding some 0.5-0.6 percentage points on the island's jobless rate.

Economists later said losses would be no more than 20,000 because many hog industry workers have other part-time jobs and since most hog processing firms have reduced work hours rather than firing staff.
Taiwan's jobless rate held close to 1.5 percent in 1991-1994 but rose to 1.79 percent in 1995 and has pushed above 3.0 percent in August, September and October 1996.
The jobless rate rose to 2.60 percent in 1996.

Officials have attributed the shift to higher joblessness to a fundamental economic shift -- a broad move toward service industries from labour-intensive manufacturing that had fuelled Taiwan's dramatic economic development in earlier decades.
-- Taipei Newsroom (2-5080815)
